headline: The Ledge Went Quiet at Noon and Loud at Midnight — First Bonito Scouts Showing
subhead: Bass have slid deep and nocturnal off the island's structure, but the tide is building toward the new moon and the first albie-and-bonito scouts are already testing the rips.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it — stepped out on the porch at Payne's dock around five in the morning and the air had that flat, heavy stillness that usually means the water underneath is doing something different than the surface lets on. No wind to speak of, glassy out past the breakwater, and the gulls weren't working. That's the tell on this island. When the birds go quiet at first light in August, the bait's not up top — it's down deep, and the bass are down there with it.

That's exactly the pattern we've been in for the better part of two weeks now. Surface temps around the island are sitting in that upper-60s to low-70s range, warm enough that the stripers don't want any part of the shallow reef tops during daylight. They've pulled off the crown of the Southwest Ledge and down into the 40- to 60-foot water along the edges, and mostly they're not feeding hard until the sun's well down. I've had my best luck the last few nights working the Ledge on the last two hours of the ebb, drifting live eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — 3 to 4 ounces depending on how hard it's running. Same story out at the North Rip. Daytime it's dead quiet up top, but drop a bunker chunk down into 50 feet on the drop-off after dark and you'll know pretty quick if there's a 30-pounder sitting on that structure. Pulled a 38-pound fish off there Tuesday night on a whole fresh bunker, and the guy fishing next to me on the charter boat had one push 40 an hour later. They're there. You just have to fish the clock, not the calendar.

Bluefish are the daylight consolation prize right now, and they're not shy about it. Bait pushes have been moving through off the southwest corner and around Southeast Light, and when you find the birds working — which, unlike the bass pattern, they will do for blues — you can load the boat fast. Deep-diving stainless spoons in chrome or chartreuse trolled through the melee, or if you want to have some fun with it, cast poppers right into the boil. Fish are running 4 to 8 pounds, plenty of teeth, and they'll keep kids and visiting anglers happy while the bass sulk through the heat.

Fluke fishing has stayed the most dependable thing on the island, which isn't flashy but it's honest work and it's putting dinner on the table. The sandy stretches off the Coast Guard Channel and the drop near the Great Salt Pond entrance have been giving up a steady mix of keepers and shorts on the drift — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along bottom on the last of the incoming. We said last week the fluke bite would stay steady rather than blow up into anything blitz-like, and that's held true — no explosion, just solid, repeatable numbers if you cover the right bottom.

Now for the part I've had my eye on since late July — the albie and bonito watch. We flagged Block Island as one of the top zones on the coastwide radar for the season's first real push, and this week the scouts started showing. Nothing you'd call an arrival yet, but a few boats working bait around the rips off the southwest corner have had single fish crash bait and vanish just as fast — the classic scout pattern before the school shows up in force. The new moon builds through August 12, and that's the trigger everybody on this dock is watching for. Bigger tides mean harder current through the Ledge and the North Rip, which stacks bait tighter against the structure and usually is what flips the switch on these fish. If you're rigging up for it, keep a light spinning outfit ready with small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks or Albie Snax in bone or pink — because when they show, the window can close in twenty minutes.

Porgies have been a nice quiet bite for anyone wanting an easy afternoon — Point Judith and the drop-offs along Narragansett Bay's outer edge have been thick with scup on squid strips and sandworms over mixed bottom, small hooks, light tackle, kids' rods. Nothing glamorous, but it's fun fishing and the freezer appreciates it.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the bass pattern to shift much in the next few days — the water needs either a real cooling trend or a stronger blow to push surface temps down enough to get these fish moving in daylight again, and I don't see that in the forecast yet. So if you're chasing stripers, plan around the tide, not the sun — first hour of dusk through the top of the flood has been the sweet spot on the Ledge all week. But keep one rod rigged light and ready for a run to the rips if word comes across the radio that something's busting on top. That first real bonito school of the year can show up with almost no warning once the moon starts pulling harder, and out here, being ten minutes late usually means you missed it.
